title: Toward a Durable Compromise on Discipline Disparities? September 4, 2026
author: Mike Petrilli
source: Schooled by Mike Petrilli / Fordham Institute (schooledbymikepetrilli.substack.com),
summary: Mike Petrilli uses the whiplash history of federal school-discipline civil-rights guidance — reversed by the Trump administration in 2018, reinstated by Biden's OCR in 2023, and now reversed again with new language declaring that 'the consideration of race in student discipline is race discrimination' — to argue that the underlying problem isn't which side is right, but that federal policy keeps 'lurching wildly from one presidential administration to the next' with no durable resolution. Rather than picking a side in the ideologically polarized fight, Petrilli proposes Congress legislate a compromise that would survive changes in administration, and floats two concrete options: either removing discipline-disparity statistics from civil-rights enforcement entirely and focusing federal attention only on specific discrimination complaints, or keeping the Obama/Biden disparity-monitoring approach but only after controlling for socioeconomic status, since SES 'can explain most (though no, not all)' of America's discipline disparities. His argument for the SES-adjusted approach is that it would redirect federal scrutiny toward districts with disparities that persist even after accounting for poverty — the cases where systemic discrimination is genuinely more likely — rather than flagging every district with a raw disparity regardless of cause. The piece closes as an open invitation rather than a settled proposal, explicitly asking readers whether either option could earn 'begrudging' support from both the left and right.
points: Petrilli's framing of 12 years of reversing federal guidance as a 'game of ping-pong' reframes the discipline-disparities debate away from 'which side is correct' toward a shared, cross-partisan problem: policy instability itself is harming schools regardless of the substantive merits of either position.

His SES-adjustment proposal — investigating only districts with racial disparities that persist after controlling for poverty, since SES 'can explain most (though no, not all)' of the raw disparities — offers a specific methodological compromise that neither ignores race nor treats every raw disparity as proof of discrimination.

By proposing that Congress legislate a compromise 'in statute' rather than leaving the rule to executive-branch guidance, Petrilli targets the actual mechanism of the instability (guidance reversible by each new administration), not just the current administration's specific policy content.
quotes: who reported on the 'game of ping-pong' underway over the past 12 years, with federal civil rights policy lurching wildly from one presidential administration to the next.
As the new guidance puts it: 'The consideration of race in student discipline is race discrimination.'

But I wonder: Are we going to just continue playing this game of ping-pong? A much better approach would be for Congress to forge a compromise, put it in statute, and clarify the rules that educators must follow regardless of which party controls the White House.
Student SES can explain most (though no, not all) of the discipline disparities in America's schools.

The federal concern should be on districts with large racial disparities even after poverty and the like are taken into account, because those are the places where systemic discrimination is more likely to be at fault.
Is there an approach to civil rights enforcement on discipline disparities that folks on both the right and left could (begrudgingly) support?
